title: Scaloppine al marsala
subtitle: Thin chicken escalopes in marsala and mushroom sauce
excerpt: Scaloppine al marsala pairs beaten chicken escalopes with a deeply flavoured pan sauce of Marsala wine and mushrooms. The Marsala reduces quickly in the hot pan and combines with the meat juices and butter into a glossy, slightly sweet sauce. It is a faster dish than its richness suggests.
sourceNotes: Italian trattoria classic. Scaloppine al marsala originated in Sicily, where Marsala wine is produced, and spread across mainland Italy. Traditionally made with veal; this recipe uses chicken breast. Method drawn from Marcella Hazan, Essentials of Classic Italian Cooking (1992).

glossaryTerms.definition: A fortified wine from western Sicily; dry Marsala is used in savoury cooking for sauces and braises; sweet Marsala goes into desserts like zabaione and tiramisu.

content.text: is a richer version of the lemon escalope: the same beaten, floured chicken, but the sauce is built on dry Marsala and chestnut mushrooms. Use dry Marsala for this, not sweet. The sauce should taste savoury and nutty, not like a dessert.

items.prepNote: halved horizontally and beaten flat to 5 mm

content.text: Beat {{chicken-breast}} of chicken breast halves flat to 5 mm. Dust in {{plain-flour}} of seasoned flour, shaking off excess.
Heat 40 g of butter with {{olive-oil}} of olive oil in a wide frying pan over high heat. Fry the escalopes for 2 minutes per side. Transfer to a warm plate.

Add {{chestnut-mushrooms}} of sliced mushrooms to the pan and cook over high heat for 3 minutes until golden. Pour in {{fortified-marsala}} of dry Marsala. Let it bubble for 2 minutes, scraping up the pan residue. Add {{stock-chicken}} of chicken stock. Simmer for 3 minutes until the sauce coats a spoon.
Add the remaining 20 g of cold butter and swirl until melted. Return the escalopes to the pan, spoon the sauce over, and warm for 30 seconds. Serve immediately with the parsley scattered over.

items.cause: Sweet Marsala used instead of dry.
items.fix: This recipe requires dry Marsala. Sweet Marsala belongs in tiramisu, not this sauce.

items.cause: Overcooked, or the sauce was not poured back over in the final step.
items.fix: At 5 mm, 2 minutes per side is the maximum over high heat. Return the escalopes to the sauce for warmth, not for more cooking.

content.text: Scaloppine al marsala traces to Sicily, where the wine was first fortified for export in the late 18th century. The recipe spread north with the wine, and the combination of Marsala and veal became a fixture of Milanese and Roman trattoria cooking. With chicken, it remains as popular across Italy as it ever was. Serve with soft polenta or pasta with butter to soak up the sauce.
